chunks: The three ideal op-amp rules. The question: What are the three rules of an ideal opamp?
The three ideal op-amp rules are a shortcut for analyzing circuits. The inputs draw no current.
The output is a perfect voltage source: it holds its voltage whatever current is drawn.
And the gain is infinite, which with negative feedback (the output wired back to the minus input) forces the two inputs to the same voltage.
Real parts only approximate these rules.
Imagine a very picky referee who keeps changing the score until both teams are tied.
The referee cannot be stopped from correcting any gap, however small, so the teams always end up tied. The op-amp does this to its inputs, using its output as the adjustment.
The "virtual short" is the tie.
With the + input grounded and a virtual short, the minus node is at 0 volts.
The current I equals V in over R in cannot enter the op-amp (rule 1), so it flows through R f and produces V out equals -IR f .
Input impedance: how hard it is for current to flow into the input. Ideally infinite. Output impedance: ideally zero, so the output holds its voltage under load.
Open-loop gain: ideally infinite. Virtual short: the two inputs sit at the same voltage under negative feedback.
Virtual ground: a minus input held at 0 volts because the plus input is grounded.
Build an inverting amplifier with R in equals 1 kilohms and R f equals 10 kilohms, plus input grounded. Apply V in equals 0. 5 volts.
The minus input is at 0 volts by the virtual short, so the input current is 0. 5 over 1 kilohms equals 0. 5 milliamps. No current enters the op-amp, so all 0.
5 milliamps goes through R f . The output is -0. 5 milliamps times 10 kilohms equals -5 volts, a gain of -10 . That is the whole idea.
"The ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, so no current flows into the inputs; zero output impedance, so the output is an ideal voltage source; and infinite gain.
With negative feedback, infinite gain forces the difference between the inputs to zero, the virtual short, so V plus equals V - . With these I can solve a circuit with just KCL.
For an inverting amp the minus node is a virtual ground, the input current all flows through the feedback resistor, and the gain is -R f over R in ."
Quick check. Which ideal op-amp property implies that no current flows into the inputs?
